Lo, out of abundance the Father answers from heaven, to attest to the Son: "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him." So too in this: "I have glorified, and I will glorify again." How many persons seem to you here, most perverse Praxeas, but as many as there are voices? You have the Son on earth, you have the Father in heaven. This is not a separation, but a divine disposition. For the rest, we know that God is even within the depths, and exists everywhere — but by power and might. The Son too, as individual, is everywhere with him. Yet in the very oikonomia the Father willed the Son to be held on earth, but himself in heaven; to which the Son himself, looking up, both prayed and besought of the Father — to which he also taught us to pray, lifting up our hands: "Our Father, who are in heaven" — although he is also everywhere. This seat the Father willed for himself: he made the Son a little less by sending him down to earth, yet to crown him with glory and honour by taking him back into the heavens. These things he was already supplying him, saying, "I have both glorified, and I will glorify." The Son asks from the earth, the Father promises from the heavens. Why do you make both Father and Son liars? If either the Father was speaking from the heavens to the Son, when he himself was the Son on earth, or the Son was praying to the Father, when he himself was the Son in the heavens: how can it be that the Son likewise asked of himself, in asking of the Father, if the Son was the Father? Or again that the Father promised to himself, in promising to the Son, if he was the Father? So that, even if we said two divided, as you charge us with raving, it were more tolerable to preach two divided than one shifty God. Therefore the Lord now pronounced for the sake of these men: "This voice came not for my sake, but for yours" — that these too might believe both the Father and the Son, each in his own names and persons and places. But still Jesus cries out and says: "He who believes in me, believes not in me, but in him who sent me" — because through the Son one believes in the Father, and the Father is the authority for believing in the Son. "And he who beholds me, beholds him who sent me." How? Because, namely, "I have not spoken of myself, but the Father who sent me, he himself gave me commandment what I should say and what I should speak. For the Lord gives me a tongue of instruction, that I may know when it is fitting to speak the word which I speak. As the Father has said to me, so I speak." How these things were said, the evangelist — and surely so dear a disciple, John, rather than Praxeas — knew; and therefore he himself, from his own understanding, says: "But before the festival of the Passover, Jesus, knowing that all things were given to him by the Father, and that he was from God, and was going to God." But Praxeas would have the Father himself to have gone forth from himself, and to have departed to himself — so that the devil put into the heart of Judas not the betrayal of the Son, but of the Father himself. But it goes well neither with the devil nor with the heretic, since not even in the Son, his own true Son, did the devil work the betrayal. For it was the Son of God who was betrayed, who was in the Son of man, as the Scripture subjoins: "Now is the Son of man glorified, and God is glorified in him." What God? Surely not the Father, but the Word of the Father, who was in the Son of man — that is, in the flesh — in which he was already glorified by power and by word, even before, as Jesus. "And God," he says, "shall glorify him in himself" — that is, the Father the Son, whom, having him in himself, even though stretched out to earth, he shall soon, through the resurrection, with death overcome, glorify.

There were plainly those who even then did not understand. For Thomas too was for a while incredulous. "Lord," he says, "we know not where you go, and how do we know the way?" And Jesus: "I am the way, the truth, and the life; no one comes to the Father but through me; if you had known me, you would have known the Father also; but henceforth you know him, and have seen him." And we have now come to Philip, who, roused by the hope of seeing the Father, and not understanding how he had heard that the Father was seen, "Show us the Father," he says, "and it suffices us." And the Lord: "Philip, so long a time have I been with you, and you have not known me?" Whom does he say they ought to have known — for this alone must be discussed — as Father, or as Son? If as Father, let Praxeas teach that Christ, while conversing so long with them, could at any time, I will not say be understood, but even be reckoned, the Father. To us all the Scriptures — the old foretelling Christ as God's, the new as the Son of God — determine it beforehand. This was preached formerly too; this was pronounced by Christ himself; nay, even by the Father himself, openly from the heavens professing the Son and glorifying the Son: "This is my Son"; and, "I have glorified, and I will glorify." This was believed by the disciples, this not believed by the Jews. Wishing this to be believed by them, he named the Father at every hour, and put the Father forward, and honoured the Father. If it is so, then it was not the Father whom they had been ignorant of, though so long conversant with them, but the Son; and the Lord, reproaching them that he himself was unknown, whom they had not known, surely wished to be acknowledged the very one whom for so long he had reproached them with not acknowledging — that is, the Son. And it can now appear in what way it was said: "He who sees me, sees the Father also" — namely just as above, "I and the Father are one." Why? Because, "I went forth from God and came"; and, "I am the way; no one comes to the Father but through me"; and, "No one comes to me except the Father draw him"; and, "All things has the Father given me"; and, "As the Father gives life, so also the Son"; and, "If you have known me, you have known the Father also." For according to these sayings he had shown himself the Father's vicar, through whom the Father was both seen in deeds, and heard in words, and known in the Son — administering the deeds and words of the Father; because the Father is invisible, which Philip too had learned in the law, and ought to have remembered: "No man shall see God, and live." And therefore he is rebuked for desiring to see the Father, as though visible, and is instructed that the Father is made visible in the Son out of his mighty works, not out of a representation of person. In fine, if he would have the Father understood to be the same as the Son by saying, "He who sees me, sees the Father," how does he subjoin, "Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me?" For he ought to have subjoined, "Do you not believe that I am the Father?" Or to what purpose did he heighten it, if he did not make plain what he had wished understood — namely that he is the Son? Moreover, by saying, "Do you not believe that I am in the Father, and the Father in me," he rather heightened it for this very reason: that, because he had said, "He who sees me, sees the Father too," he might not be supposed the Father — which he never wished himself to be supposed, who always professed himself the Son and to have come from the Father. He therefore both made plain the conjunction of the two persons, lest the Father should be desired separately, as though visible, in sight, and that the Son might be held the representative of the Father. And none the less he interpreted this too, how the Father was in the Son, and the Son in the Father. "The words," he says, "which I speak to you, are not mine" — surely because the Father's; "but the Father abiding in me does the works." Through the works, then, of mighty deeds, and the words of teaching, the Father, abiding in the Son, is seen through those things by which he abides, and through him in whom he abides — from this very thing the property of each person appearing, while he says, "I am in the Father, and the Father in me." And indeed, "Believe," he says. What? That I am the Father? I do not think it is written so, but, "That I am in the Father, and the Father in me; or if not, believe even for the works' sake" — those works, surely, through which the Father was in the Son, seen not by sight, but by sense.

After Philip and the whole substance of this question, which is toward the end of the Gospel, they persevere in the same kind of discourse, by which Father and Son are distinguished in their own property. He promises also that he will ask the Paraclete of the Father, when he has ascended to the Father, and will send him — and indeed "another." But we have already explained in what sense "another." For the rest, "He shall take of mine," he says, just as he himself of the Father's. Thus the connection of the Father in the Son and of the Son in the Paraclete makes three cohering, one out of another. These three are one thing, not one person, just as it was said, "I and the Father are one thing" — in reference to unity of substance, not to singularity of number. Run on further, and you will find that the one whom you believe to be the Father (it being said in the Father's place, and you suppose the Father to have been the husbandman on earth) is again acknowledged in the heavens by the Son, when, looking up there, he handed over his disciples to the Father. But even if in this Gospel it is not revealed, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" and, "Father, into your hands I commit my spirit," yet after the resurrection and the glory of death overcome, the necessity of all his lowliness being now discharged, when he could now show himself the Father to so faithful a woman, who from love, not from curiosity nor from the unbelief of Thomas, had ventured to touch him, "Touch me not," he says, "for I have not yet ascended to my Father; but go to my brethren" (nay, in this too he shows himself the Son, for he would have called them sons, had he been the Father), "and tell them, I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God." Father to Father, and God to God? Or Son to Father, and Word to God? The very close of the Gospel too — for what does it set its seal upon these things written, but, "That you may believe," it says, "that Jesus Christ is the Son of God"? Therefore, whatever out of these you shall have thought can avail you toward the demonstration of one and the same Father and Son, you strive against the definitive sentence of the Gospel. For they were not written that you should believe Jesus Christ to be the Father, but the Son.

On account of one saying of Philip and the Lord's answer to him, we seem to have run through John's Gospel — lest one saying should subvert so many things plainly pronounced both before and after, and to be interpreted according to all the rest rather than against them all, even against its own sense. For the rest, not to bring in the other Gospels, which confirm faith by the Lord's nativity, it suffices that he who was to be born of the virgin was determined by the angel himself, in his announcement, the Son of God. "The Spirit of God shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore that which shall be born of you holy shall be called the Son of God." They will indeed wish to argue here too, but the truth will prevail. "Surely," they say, "the Son of God is God, and the power of the Most High is the Most High." Nor are they ashamed to throw in what, had it been so, would have been written. For whom did he fear, that he did not openly pronounce, "God shall come upon you, and the Most High shall overshadow you"? But by saying, "the Spirit of God," although it is the Spirit of God, yet not directly naming "God," he wished a portion of the whole to be understood, which was to pass into the name of Son. This Spirit of God will be the same as the Word. For just as, when John says, "The Word was made flesh," we understand the Spirit too in the mention of the Word, so here too we acknowledge the Word in the name of Spirit. For the Spirit is the substance of the Word, and the Word the operation of the Spirit, and the two are one thing. Otherwise John will profess one to have been made flesh, the angel another to be made flesh — unless the Spirit too is the Word, and the Word the Spirit. As, therefore, the Word of God is not he himself whose he is, so neither is the Spirit; and although he is called God, yet he is not himself whose he is called. No thing belonging to another is itself that to which it belongs. Plainly, when something is from another, and so is its own — while it is from it — it can be such a thing as he is too from whom it is and whose it is. And therefore the Spirit is God, and the Word is God, because from God, yet not himself from whom he is. What is "God of God," as a substantive thing, will not be God himself, but God thus far, inasmuch as it is from the substance of God himself, and inasmuch as it is a substantive thing, and as a certain portion of the whole. Much more will "the power of the Most High" not be the Most High himself, because it is not even a substantive thing, as is the Spirit, just as neither is wisdom nor providence; for these too are not substances, but accidents of each substance. Power happens to the Spirit, nor will it itself be Spirit. By these things, then, whatever they are — the Spirit of God, and the Word, and the Power — brought together upon the virgin, that which is born of her is the Son of God. This he himself testifies, even in these Gospels, straightway as a boy: "Know you not," he says, "that I must be in my Father's house?" This too Satan knew in the temptations: "If you are the Son of God." This too the demons thereafter confess: "We know who you are, the Son of God." The Father too he himself adores. He does not deny that he is acknowledged by Peter to be God's Christ. Exulting in spirit to the Father: "I confess to you," he says, "Father, that you have hidden these things from the wise." Here too he affirms that the Father is known to no one but the Son, and that the Father's Son will confess his confessors and deny his deniers before the Father; bringing in the parable of a son, not of a father, sent into the vineyard after several servants, and slain by the wicked husbandmen, and avenged by the father; he himself too being ignorant of the last day and hour, known to the Father alone; disposing the kingdom to his disciples, as he says it was disposed to himself by the Father; having power to ask the Father for legions of angels to his aid, if he would; crying out that God had forsaken him; placing his spirit in the Father's hands; and, after the resurrection, promising to send to his disciples the promise of the Father; and last of all commanding that they should baptize into the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, not into one. For not once, but thrice, at each name, into the several persons, are we baptized.

And why should I linger over things so manifest, when I ought to attack those by which they seek to overshadow the manifest? For, hemmed in on every side concerning the distinction of Father and Son — which, with the conjunction abiding, we so dispose, as of sun and ray, and spring and river, yet through the individual number of two and three — they attempt to interpret it in still another way, to their own view none the less: so that they distinguish both in one person, Father and Son, teaching that the Son is the flesh — that is, man, that is, Jesus — but the Father is the spirit, that is, God, that is, Christ. And they who contend that Father and Son are one and the same, begin now rather to divide them than to unite them. For if Jesus is one, Christ another, then Son will be one, Father another, because Jesus is the Son, and Christ the Father. Such a monarchy they have perhaps learned from Valentinus, to make two — Jesus and Christ. But this thrust of theirs too has already been beaten back by what was treated before — namely that "the Word of God," or "the Spirit of God," and "the power of the Most High," is the name given to him whom they make the Father. For these are not themselves those whose they are called, but from him and his. And yet in another way too they will be refuted in this chapter. "Lo," they say, "it was preached by the angel: Therefore that which is born holy shall be called the Son of God. The flesh, then, was born; the flesh, then, will be the Son of God." Nay, it was said concerning the Spirit of God. For surely the virgin conceived of the Holy Spirit, and what she conceived, that she bore; that therefore was to be born which was conceived and to be brought forth — that is, the Spirit, whose name too shall be called Emmanuel, which is interpreted, "God with us." But the flesh is not God, that of it should be said, "It shall be called the holy Son of God"; rather he who was born in it is God, of whom the psalm too: "Since God was born man in her, and built her up by the will of the Father." What God was born in her? The Word, and the Spirit, who by the Word was born of the Father's will. Therefore the Word in the flesh — while we must also inquire concerning this, in what way the Word was made flesh, whether as transfigured in the flesh, or as having put on the flesh. Nay, as having put it on. For the rest, it is necessary to believe God unchangeable and unformable, as eternal. But transfiguration is the destruction of what was before. For everything, whatever is transfigured into something else, ceases to be what it was, and begins to be what it was not. But God neither ceases to be nor can be anything else. The Word, however, is God, and "the Word of the Lord abides for ever" — by persevering, namely, in his own form. And if it is not in him to be configured, it follows that he should be understood to have been made flesh thus: while he comes to be in flesh, and is manifested and seen and handled through flesh; because the rest too demand to be so taken. For if the Word was made flesh out of a transfiguration and change of substance, then Jesus will be one substance out of two — out of flesh and spirit — a certain mixture, as electrum out of gold and silver; and he begins to be neither gold, that is, spirit, nor silver, that is, flesh, while the one is changed by the other, and a third something is produced. Then neither will Jesus be God; for the Word ceased to be, who was made flesh: nor flesh, that is, man; for the flesh is not properly flesh, because it was the Word. Thus, out of both, he is neither; he is something else, a third far different from either. But in truth we find him directly set forth both God and man — this very psalm suggesting it: "Since God was born man in her, he built her up by the will of the Father" — certainly throughout, both Son of God and Son of man, since both God and man, without doubt distinct according to each substance in its own property, because neither is the Word anything other than God, nor the flesh anything other than man. So too the Apostle teaches concerning each of his substances. "Who was made," he says, "of the seed of David." This will be the man and Son of man, who was determined the Son of God according to the Spirit. This will be the God and the Word, the Son of God. We see a double condition, not confused but conjoined, in one person — God and the man Jesus. (Concerning Christ I defer.) And so the property of each substance is preserved, that the Spirit carried on its own things in him — that is, mighty works and operations and signs — and the flesh discharged its own passions, hungering under the devil, thirsting under the Samaritan woman, weeping for Lazarus, troubled even unto death, and finally even dying. But if it were a third something compounded out of both, like electrum, the documents of each substance would not appear so distinct. But the Spirit would have done fleshly things, and the flesh spiritual, by transference; or neither fleshly nor spiritual, but of some third form out of the mixture; nay, either the Word would have died, or the flesh would not have died, had the Word been turned into flesh — for either the flesh would have been immortal, or the Word mortal. But because both substances acted distinctly, each in its own condition, therefore both their works and their issues befell them. Learn then, with Nicodemus: "Because that which is born of the flesh is flesh, and that which is of the Spirit is spirit." Neither does flesh become spirit, nor spirit flesh. They can plainly be in one. Of these Jesus consists: man of the flesh, God of the Spirit; whom then the angel, from that part by which he was Spirit, pronounced the Son of God, reserving for the flesh to be called the Son of man. So too the Apostle, by calling him a mediator of God and of men, confirmed each substance. Lastly, you who interpret the Son of God as flesh, show who is the Son of man. Or will it perhaps be the Spirit? But you will have the Spirit be the Father himself, because "God is spirit" — as though the Spirit of God were not also "spirit," just as the Word too is God and the Word of God.

So you make Christ the Father, most foolish one, you who do not even inspect the very force of this name — if indeed Christ is a name, and not rather an appellation; for it signifies "the anointed." And "anointed" is no more a name than "clothed" or "shod" — a thing incidental to a name. Or you, if from some argument Jesus were also called "the clothed," as he is called Christ from the sacrament of anointing, would you likewise call Jesus the Son of God, but believe the clothed to be the Father? Now concerning Christ. If the Father is Christ, the Father is anointed, and surely by another. Or, if by himself, prove it. But the Acts of the Apostles do not so teach, in that outcry of the Church to God: "For there gathered together in this city against your holy Son, whom you have anointed, Herod and Pilate with the nations." Thus they attested both that Jesus is the Son of God and that the Son was anointed by the Father. Therefore Jesus will be the same as Christ, who was anointed by the Father — not the Father, who anointed the Son. So too Peter: "Let all the house of Israel therefore know most surely, that God has made him both Lord and Christ — that is, anointed — this Jesus, whom you crucified." And John marks as a liar even him who shall deny that Jesus is the Christ, but, on the contrary, as born of God everyone who shall believe that Jesus is the Christ. Wherefore he also exhorts that we believe in the name of his Son Jesus Christ, that there may be fellowship for us with the Father and his Son Jesus Christ. So too Paul everywhere sets God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ. When he writes to the Romans, he gives thanks to God through our Lord Jesus Christ; when to the Galatians, he asserts himself an apostle not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father. And you have all his writings, which pronounce after this manner, and set forth two — God and the Father, and our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of the Father; and that Jesus himself is Christ, in the other name too the Son of God. For henceforth, by that right by which each name belongs to one — that is, to the Son of God — the one also without the other belongs to the same. And whether "Jesus" alone is set down, "Christ" too is understood, because Jesus is anointed; or whether "Christ" only, the same is also Jesus, because the anointed is Jesus. Of which names the one is proper, which was imposed by the angel, the other incidental, which befits from the anointing — provided always that Christ is the Son, not the Father. Lastly, how blind is he who does not understand, even in the name of Christ, that another God is portended, if he ascribes the name of Christ to the Father. For if Christ the Father is God, who says, "I ascend to my Father and your Father, and my God and your God" — surely he shows another Father and God above himself. If likewise the Father is Christ, then another is he who "fixes the thunder firm, and frames the spirit, and announces his Christ to men." And if "the kings of the earth stood by, and the rulers were gathered together against his Christ," then another will be the Lord against whose Christ kings and rulers were gathered. And if, "Thus says the Lord to my lord Christ," then another will be the Lord who speaks to the Father of Christ. And when the Apostle writes, "That the God of our Lord Jesus Christ may give you the Spirit of wisdom and knowledge," then another will be the God of Christ Jesus, the bestower of spiritual graces. Certainly, not to wander through all, he who raised Christ is also to raise our mortal bodies; and so another will be the raiser than a dead Father and a raised Father, if Christ, who died, is the Father.

Let it fall silent, let it fall silent, that blasphemy. Let it suffice to say that Christ the Son of God died — and this, because it is so written. For the Apostle too, not without weight, in pronouncing Christ dead, adds, "according to the Scriptures," that he might soften the hardness of the pronouncement by the authority of the Scriptures and avert offence from the hearer. Yet, since two substances are reckoned in Christ Jesus, the divine and the human, and it is agreed that the divine is immortal, as that which is human is mortal, it appears in what sense he calls him dead — that is, as flesh and man and Son of man, not as Spirit and Word and Son of God. By saying, in fine, "Christ died" — that is, "the anointed" — he shows that what was anointed died — that is, the flesh. "Therefore," you say, "we too, saying the same with the same reasoning as you, do not blaspheme the Lord God in respect of the Son; for we say him dead not of the divine, but of the human substance." But you do blaspheme, not only because you say the Father died, but also because you say he was crucified. For by the curse of the crucified, which by the law falls upon the Son (because Christ was made a curse for us, not the Father), by turning Christ into the Father, you blaspheme against the Father. But we, in saying that Christ was crucified, do not curse him, but report the curse of the law — since neither did the Apostle blaspheme in saying this. As, then, what is fitting to be said of one is said without blasphemy, so what is not fitting is blasphemy, if it be said. Therefore the Father did not even suffer-with the Son. Plainly, fearing direct blasphemy against the Father, they hope to diminish it in this way, granting now that Father and Son are two, if the Son indeed thus suffers, but the Father suffers-with him. Foolish in this too. For what is to "suffer-with" but to suffer along with another? Moreover, if the Father is impassible, surely he is also incapable of suffering-with; or, if capable of suffering-with, surely passible. You profit him nothing even by this fear of yours. You are afraid to call passible him whom you call capable of suffering-with. But the Father is as incapable of suffering-with as the Son too is impassible, from that condition by which he is God. But how did the Son suffer, if the Father did not suffer-with him? He is separated from the Son, not from God. For even a river, if it is fouled by some turbulence, although it runs as one substance from the spring, nor is severed from the spring, yet the river's harm will not reach the spring; and although it is the water of the spring that suffers in the river, while it suffers not in the spring but in the river, it is not the spring that suffers, but the river, which is from the spring. So too the Spirit of God, whatever it may suffer in the Son, because it would not suffer in the Father, but in the Son, the Father would not seem to have suffered. But it suffices that the Spirit of God suffered nothing in its own name, because, if it suffered anything, it suffered in the Son. It was indeed another matter that the Father should suffer with the Son in the flesh. This too has been treated. Nor will anyone deny it; since neither can we suffer for God, unless the Spirit of God be in us, who also speaks concerning us the things that belong to confession — not itself, however, suffering, but supplying the power to suffer.

Otherwise, if you go further, I shall be able to answer you more harshly, and to set you at odds with the Lord's own pronouncement, so that I may say: what do you ask about this? You have him crying out in the passion, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Therefore either the Son was suffering, forsaken by the Father, and the Father did not suffer, who forsook the Son; or, if it was the Father who was suffering, to what God was he crying out? But this voice of flesh and soul — that is, of man, not of the Word nor the Spirit, that is, not of God — was uttered for this purpose: to show God impassible, who so forsook the Son, in that he handed over his manhood unto death. This the Apostle too perceived, writing: "If the Father spared not the Son." This Isaiah also pronounced before: "And the Lord handed him over for our offences." So he forsook, in not sparing; so he forsook, in handing over. For the rest, the Father did not forsake the Son, into whose hands the Son committed his own spirit. In fine, he committed it, and at once died; for, the Spirit abiding in the flesh, the flesh cannot die at all. Thus to be forsaken by the Father was, for the Son, to die. The Son therefore both dies and is raised again by the Father, according to the Scriptures. The Son ascended into the heights of the heavens, who also descended into the lower parts of the earth. He sits at the Father's right hand; not the Father at his own. Him Stephen, when he is stoned, sees still standing at the right hand of God — to sit thereafter, until the Father put all his enemies under his feet. He too is to come again upon the clouds of heaven, such as he also ascended. He meanwhile poured out the gift received from the Father, the Holy Spirit, the third name of the godhead and the third stage of the majesty, the proclaimer of the one monarchy, but also the interpreter of the oikonomia, if anyone shall receive the words of his new prophecy, and the guide into all truth, which is in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, according to the Christian mystery.

For the rest, it is a matter of Jewish faith so to believe in one God as to refuse to number the Son with him, and after the Son the Spirit. For what shall there be between us and them but this difference? What is the work of the Gospel, what the substance of the New Testament, setting the law and the prophets up to John, if from that point Father and Son and Spirit, believed as three, do not constitute one God? So God willed to renew the mystery, that the One might be believed in a new way through the Son and the Spirit — that now openly God might be known in his own proper names and persons, who formerly, preached through the Son and the Spirit, was not understood. Let the antichrists, then, look to it, who deny the Father and the Son. For they deny the Father, when they say the same is the Son, and they deny the Son, when they believe the same is the Father — giving to them what they are not, taking away what they are. But whoever shall confess Christ the Son of God, not the Father, God abides in him, and he in God. Unless we believe the testimony of God, by which he testified concerning his Son. He who has not the Son, neither has life. But he has not the Son, who believes him to be other than the Son.
